title: Find the Highest Altitude
description: Brute force to optimized: resumming from the start at every point versus a running altitude paired with a running maximum.

blocks.text: There is a biker going on a road trip. The trip consists of n plus 1 points at different altitudes, starting at point 0 with altitude 0. Given an integer array gain of length n, where gain[i] is the net change in altitude between point i and point i plus 1, return the highest altitude reached anywhere on the trip.

blocks.caption: Carry a running altitude forward and keep the highest point touched along the way

Given an integer array gain of length n, where gain[i] is the net change in altitude between point i and point i plus 1, return the highest altitude reached anywhere on the trip.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tracking a Hiker's Elevation Gain Point by Point
blocks.text: Like a hiking app that logs elevation change between each waypoint and reports the single highest elevation reached anywhere on the trail, without needing a full topographic survey redone at every waypoint.

blocks.caption: Update the elevation one waypoint at a time, keeping track of the highest point touched so far

blocks.text: With a single positive gain, the altitude simply rises from 0 to 100 at the next point, making the highest altitude trivially 100.

Before summing each point's altitude independently, notice that altitude is a running quantity that only ever changes by one gain value at a time, and the question only asks for the single largest value that running quantity ever reaches.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The altitude at point i is completely determined by adding up every gain value from the very first point up through point i, since each gain describes exactly the change between two consecutive points.

Observation 2: This is precisely a prefix sum over the gain array, with one extra detail: the sequence of altitudes has one more entry than gain itself, since it starts with the fixed value 0 before any gain has been applied.

Observation 3: Finding the highest altitude does not require storing every altitude value at all; it only requires knowing the single largest one seen, which can be tracked incrementally alongside the running altitude itself, updated the moment a new altitude exceeds it.

Observation 4: So the entire problem collapses to one single pass: maintain a running altitude starting at 0, update it by each gain value in order, and keep a running maximum of every altitude value seen along the way, including the very starting altitude of 0.

Whenever a problem describes a sequence of values building up from a fixed starting point through incremental changes, and asks for some aggregate, like the maximum, over that whole built-up sequence, compute the running value and the running aggregate together in one single pass, no separate storage needed.
This is prefix sums combined with a simple running-maximum tracker, a pairing that reappears constantly whenever a cumulative quantity needs to be both built and summarized in the same pass.
For every point, independently sum all the gains leading up to it from the very start, then compare all of these computed altitudes to find the largest one.

items: For each point from 1 to n, sum every gain value leading up to it, from the very start, to get that point's altitude.
Track the largest altitude found, including the starting altitude of 0.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: highest starts at 0, not at some arbitrary sentinel, since the very first point's altitude, 0, is always itself a valid candidate for the highest altitude, even if every gain is negative.
The loop runs over every point after the starting point, since the starting altitude is already accounted for by highest's initial value.
Each point's altitude is recomputed completely independently of the altitude computed for the previous point, deliberately not reusing any previous work.

blocks.text: Every point's true altitude is directly computed from the start, so the correct highest altitude is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the altitude at point i costs O(i) to compute and this repeats for every point.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the loop variables.

Limitation: the altitude at point i and the altitude at point i minus 1 differ by exactly one value, gain[i-1], so recomputing the full sum from scratch at every point throws away nearly all of the previous computation.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force recomputes almost identical overlapping sums at every single point, when in reality each point's altitude is just the previous point's altitude with one more gain value applied on top. Carrying a single running altitude forward, updating it by exactly one gain value per step, reconstructs every altitude the biker ever actually reaches without redoing any of the earlier addition. The only remaining piece is remembering the largest of those altitudes as they are generated, a comparison performed once per step rather than a separate scan over any stored history, including a comparison against the very starting altitude of 0 before any gain has even been applied.

Maintain a single running altitude, starting at 0. For every gain value in order, add it to the running altitude, and after each update, compare the new altitude to the highest one seen so far, keeping the larger of the two.
Carry the altitude forward one gain at a time, comparing against a running highest at every step.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single forward pass.
Space: O(1) extra.

Every altitude the biker ever reaches, including the very starting altitude of 0, is visited in order during this single pass, since the running altitude is updated by exactly one gain value at a time, in the exact sequence the trip actually occurs. Comparing the running highest against every one of these altitudes as they are generated, not after the fact, guarantees that by the time the last gain value has been processed, the running highest correctly holds the true maximum across the entire trip.

items: highest is initialized to 0 before the loop begins, directly representing the starting altitude as the first candidate for the maximum.
altitude is updated by adding exactly one gain value per iteration, mirroring the biker moving from one point to the very next one.
The comparison against highest is evaluated immediately after each update, ensuring every altitude the biker ever reaches gets compared against the running best.
No array of altitudes is ever built or stored, since only the single maximum value is ultimately needed, not the full history of every altitude visited.

blocks.text: This problem is a clean, small-scale example of pairing a running prefix sum with a running maximum, both maintained together in one pass instead of built and scanned separately.

items: Forgetting to include the starting altitude of 0 as a candidate for the highest point, especially when every gain value happens to be negative, which would make 0 the correct answer.
Recomputing each altitude from scratch instead of carrying the running total forward, reintroducing the unnecessary quadratic cost.
Comparing against the running highest before updating the running altitude, which would compare the previous point's altitude a second time instead of the newly reached one.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Every gain value is negative","The starting altitude of 0 correctly remains the highest point, since the biker never rises above where they started"],["A single gain value","The highest altitude is simply the larger of 0, the start, and that one gain value applied"]]}

items: Mention explicitly that this is a prefix sum problem in disguise, tracking a running maximum alongside the running total, since recognizing that combination immediately suggests the one-pass solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Track a cumulative value built up from a fixed starting point, and report the maximum or minimum reached along the way" points toward a prefix sum plus a running best-so-far comparison, both maintained together in one single pass.

items: How would you also report at which point the highest altitude occurred, not just its value? Track the index alongside the running highest, updating both together whenever a new maximum is found.

What if you needed the highest altitude reached within some subrange of the trip, queried repeatedly? Precompute the full array of altitudes once, a true prefix sum array, then answer each subrange query using a range-maximum structure like a sparse table, built once ahead of time.

How does this connect to Kadane's Algorithm? Both maintain one running value across a single pass while tracking a running best, though Kadane's Algorithm additionally resets its running value under certain conditions, which this problem's running altitude never does.
Same "carry a running total forward" technique as Running Sum of 1d Array, just paired here with a running maximum instead of building the full output array.
Same "one pass builds and summarizes a cumulative quantity together" idea as Kadane's Algorithm, the foundational maximum-subarray-sum technique.
Same "the starting or empty state is itself a valid candidate" consideration as Find Pivot Index's index-0 edge case, where a boundary condition must not be overlooked.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (running altitude plus running max): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Running cumulative total combined with a running maximum, both maintained in a single pass

Core Idea: Each altitude is the previous altitude plus one gain value, and the highest altitude is simply the largest value seen while building that running total, including the starting altitude itself
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A cumulative sequence and its maximum can be tracked together in one pass, with no need to store the sequence itself
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Climb one gain at a time, keep the highest point touched, and remember the starting line counts too
